lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Life Cycle and Economic Importance of the Anopheles Mosquito

pages.body:
Malaria kills hundreds of thousands of people every year, more than 90% of them in Africa. In Ghana, it is the leading cause of illness and one of the leading causes of death, especially in children under five. One small mosquito — the female Anopheles — is responsible. Understanding its life cycle is the first step to controlling it.

- Have you ever been ill with malaria? What were the symptoms?
- Where do mosquitoes breed in your community?
- Why do you think only the female Anopheles and not the male can transmit malaria?

> **DEFINITION** **Vector:** an organism that carries and transmits a pathogen (disease-causing organism) from one host to another without itself being harmed by the pathogen. **Pathogen:** an organism or agent that causes disease. The malaria pathogen is Plasmodium falciparum (a protist). **Metamorphosis:** a biological process of transformation from an immature form to an adult form in distinct stages. Mosquitoes undergo complete metamorphosis: egg → larva → pupa → adult.

pages.title: The life cycle of the Anopheles mosquito
pages.body: The Anopheles mosquito undergoes complete metamorphosis — it passes through four distinct stages, each with a different body form and lifestyle. The first three stages (egg, larva and pupa) are all aquatic, meaning they live in water. Only the adult stage is terrestrial (lives on land).

Stage 1: Egg. The female Anopheles mosquito lays her eggs on the surface of still or slow-moving water. Unlike the eggs of the housefly, Anopheles eggs are laid singly (one at a time), not in rafts. Each egg has small float structures called floats on each side that keep it at the water surface, where oxygen is available. Anopheles eggs are usually laid in small pools of clean water — this distinguishes Anopheles from Culex mosquitoes, which prefer stagnant polluted water. The eggs hatch within 1 to 3 days depending on temperature.

Stage 2: Larva. The larva (also called a wriggler) lives just at or below the water surface. It breathes through a small breathing tube (spiracle) on its body — but importantly, the Anopheles larva rests parallel to the water surface, unlike Culex larvae that hang at an angle. This is a key identification feature. The larva feeds on algae, bacteria and organic matter in the water by brushing food particles into its mouth. The larva moults (sheds its skin) four times — these growth stages are called instars. After four moults, it develops into a pupa.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Life Cycle and Economic Importance of the Anopheles Mosquito (part 3)

pages.body: Stage 3: Pupa. The pupa (also called a tumbler) is also aquatic but does not feed. It is active and can move by tumbling — curling and straightening its body to move through water. The pupa breathes through two horn-like breathing tubes (trumpets) on its head end. Inside the pupal case, the body of the adult mosquito is forming. This stage lasts 2 to 3 days.

Stage 4: Adult. The adult emerges from the pupal case at the water surface, rests briefly while its wings dry and harden, then flies off. Adult male Anopheles mosquitoes feed only on plant nectar and fruit juice. They do not bite. Adult female mosquitoes also feed on plant nectar, but they additionally need a blood meal from a mammal to obtain the protein needed to develop their eggs. It is this blood feeding that makes the female dangerous — if she bites an infected person, she picks up Plasmodium parasites; if she later bites a healthy person, she transmits the parasite.

The female Anopheles is distinguished from other mosquitoes by her resting position: she holds her body at a steep angle to the surface she lands on, with her abdomen pointing upward. The Culex mosquito holds its body parallel to the surface. This angle — called the resting pose — is a useful identification feature in the field.

pages.title: Economic importance of the Anopheles mosquito
pages.body:
The most significant economic impact of the Anopheles mosquito is negative — through the transmission of malaria. Malaria costs Ghana billions of cedis each year in healthcare costs, lost productivity and reduced school attendance. Workers miss days of work and farmers miss critical periods of cultivation. Parents spend money on medicines. Hospitals divert resources from other illnesses to treating malaria cases.

However, mosquitoes also have some positive ecological roles. Adult mosquitoes — both male and female — feed on plant nectar and are minor pollinators of some flowering plants. Mosquito larvae serve as an important food source for fish, aquatic insects, frogs and other organisms in freshwater ecosystems. The removal of all mosquitoes from an ecosystem would affect food webs, particularly those of freshwater fish.

pages.body:
Malaria has been present in Ghana for thousands of years. In the 19th century, it killed so many European visitors that West Africa was called 'the white man's grave'. Today, despite advances in medicine, malaria still kills hundreds of Ghanaian children every day. Understanding how the parasite moves from mosquito to human — and what we can do to stop it — is one of the most important topics in Basic 8 science.

- What do you know about how malaria is treated in your family or community?
- Have you seen a mosquito net? Does your family use one?
- What do you think happens inside your body when you are infected with malaria?

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: How the female Anopheles transmits Plasmodium to humans

pages.title: How the female Anopheles transmits Plasmodium to humans
pages.body:
Malaria is caused by a microscopic, single-celled parasite called Plasmodium. In Ghana, the most common and dangerous species is Plasmodium falciparum. The parasite has a complex life cycle that involves two hosts: the female Anopheles mosquito and the human being.

The transmission cycle begins when a female Anopheles mosquito bites a person who is already infected with malaria. As she feeds on blood, she takes in Plasmodium parasites (in a stage called gametocytes) along with the blood. Inside the mosquito's stomach, the male and female gametocytes fuse and the parasite undergoes sexual reproduction, producing a new form (sporozoites) that migrates to the mosquito's salivary glands. This development inside the mosquito takes about 10 to 14 days.

The infected mosquito then bites a healthy person. As she injects saliva to prevent blood from clotting, she also injects sporozoites into the person's bloodstream. The sporozoites travel rapidly to the liver, where they invade liver cells and multiply. After 8 to 30 days, they burst out of the liver cells and enter the bloodstream, where they invade red blood cells. Inside the red blood cells, they multiply again, eventually causing the cells to burst. This releases more parasites and toxins into the blood, causing the sudden fever, chills and shaking that are the classic symptoms of malaria.

The symptoms of malaria are therefore caused by the destruction of red blood cells and the release of toxins. The cyclic nature of the fever (occurring every 48 or 72 hours in different species) reflects the synchronised cycle of red blood cell destruction. Severe malaria can lead to anaemia (from the destruction of red blood cells), cerebral malaria (when parasites block blood vessels in the brain) and organ failure. Children under five and pregnant women are the most vulnerable.

pages.title: Controlling malaria in Ghana
pages.body:
Ghana uses multiple strategies to control malaria, combining individual, community and national-level interventions.

Insecticide-treated bed nets (ITBNs) are one of the most effective and widely used tools against malaria in Ghana. Sleeping under a bed net prevents mosquito bites during the night, when Anopheles mosquitoes are most active. The insecticide on the net kills mosquitoes that land on it, providing protection beyond just the person sleeping under it.

Indoor residual spraying (IRS) involves spraying the inside walls of houses with long-lasting insecticides. Mosquitoes rest on walls after feeding, and the insecticide kills them. The Ghana Health Service coordinates IRS campaigns in high-malaria areas.

Elimination of breeding sites reduces the number of mosquitoes that can develop. This includes removing standing water (filling puddles, unclogging drains, covering water storage containers, removing old tyres), which are all potential breeding sites for Anopheles mosquitoes.

Larviciding involves applying safe biological or chemical agents to water bodies where mosquito larvae are found, killing the larvae before they develop into adults.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Malaria: Impact of Anopheles and Control Measures (part 4)

pages.body:
Antimalarial medicines play two roles: treatment of infected individuals with artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs), and preventive use in high-risk groups. Pregnant women in Ghana receive preventive doses of sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP) through antenatal care. Children under five receive seasonal malaria chemoprevention (SMC) in high-risk areas.

The RTS,S/AS01 malaria vaccine (Mosquirix) is now being rolled out in Ghana as part of a pilot programme. While not 100% effective, it provides an additional layer of protection in children under five, significantly reducing the number of severe malaria cases.

Community education is essential. When communities understand the life cycle and transmission of malaria, they are better able to implement prevention measures consistently. Eliminating breeding sites requires collective action — a single uncovered water container can produce hundreds of mosquitoes per week.

> **Did you know?** Ghana was one of the first countries in the world to introduce the RTS,S/AS01 malaria vaccine in a national programme, in collaboration with the WHO. The vaccine targets Plasmodium falciparum, the deadliest malaria species, and provides about 30% protection against severe malaria — a significant public health achievement alongside other prevention tools.

The community has high rates of malaria, many uncovered water storage containers, blocked drains and many households without bed nets. Design a comprehensive malaria control plan for this community. Malaria transmission diagram: Draw a detailed diagram showing the complete malaria transmission cycle. Include: the healthy person, the infected person, the female Anopheles mosquito, the stages of Plasmodium inside the mosquito, and the stages inside the human body. Use arrows to show the direction of transmission. Label every stage and add a brief explanation beside each label.

Community malaria control poster: Design an educational poster for display in a community health centre. The poster should include: a simple life cycle diagram of the Anopheles mosquito, three ways malaria is transmitted, four prevention measures, and the message 'Malaria is preventable'. Make the poster clear and visually engaging.

Debate on malaria control: Organise a class debate on the following question: 'Which single malaria control strategy would have the greatest impact in Ghana — bed nets, indoor spraying, breeding site elimination or vaccination?' Each group argues for one strategy. After the debate, the class votes on the most convincing argument and writes an individual reflection explaining their vote.

pages.body:
| **Word** | **What it means** |
|---|---|
| Vector | An organism that carries and transmits a pathogen from one host to another |
| Pathogen | An organism or agent that causes disease |
| Plasmodium falciparum | The most dangerous malaria parasite in Ghana; a eukaryotic protist |
| Anopheles | The genus of mosquito that transmits Plasmodium; only the female bites humans |
| Metamorphosis | Biological transformation through distinct stages (egg, larva, pupa, adult) |
| Larva (wriggler) | The aquatic, feeding stage of the mosquito that breathes at the water surface |
| Pupa (tumbler) | The aquatic, non-feeding transformation stage of the mosquito |
| Sporozoite | The stage of Plasmodium injected into humans by an infected mosquito |
| Gametocyte | The stage of Plasmodium taken up by a mosquito when she bites an infected person |
| Instar | One of the growth stages between moults in a larva |
| ITNB | Insecticide-Treated Bed Net — net coated with insecticide to prevent mosquito bites |
| IRS | Indoor Residual Spraying — spraying insecticide on house walls to kill resting mosquitoes |
| ACT | Artemisinin-based Combination Therapy — the standard antimalarial treatment in Ghana |
| RTS,S vaccine | The malaria vaccine (Mosquirix) approved and being rolled out in Ghana |
| Larvicide | A substance applied to water to kill mosquito larvae |
